title: POC Weekly: Harmonics Latency Tuning & Stream/Seqlen Review
summary: Week 4 sync for the Harmonics POC: reviewed TTFT improvements from prefix caching + microbatching, streaming jitter investigation, sequence-length dependent kernel selection experiments, and next steps for a short on-site microburst test. Agreement to try a hybrid kernel path for seqlen > 1024 and run a 2-hour production shadow with hedging enabled.

Microburst/hedging test plan and expected metrics

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-26 15:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood), Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE), Jordan Meyers (NimbleScale VP Eng), Lina Torres (NimbleScale SRE), Harold Kim (NimbleScale ML)
---
[00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick check — can people hear me ok?
[00:06] Jordan: yeah, loud and clear. we're on a weird wifi but fine.
[00:10] Alex: awesome. agenda — quick results recap from the last run, streaming jitter root-cause triage, seqlen/kernels, and then decide on the microburst shadow next steps. any additions?
[00:20] Lina: maybe a short note on SLOs — we saw a tail spike last night at 3am so want to confirm mitigation path.
[00:26] Priya: noted, we'll pull the tail logs. I'll start with the TTFT numbers from Friday's profile.
[00:30] Priya: ok so for the baseline 512 token median request the TTFT dropped about 18% when we enabled prefix cache + tiny microbatch (batch size 4 continuous). median went from 78ms to 64ms. p50 p90 improved, p99 still shows occasional 340ms outliers.
[00:48] Harold: interesting — those outliers correspond to longer seqlen samples? I remember some of our customer prompts hit 1.2k occasionally.
[00:55] Priya: yes partially. p99 correlates with seqlen > 1024 and when the KV cache miss rate increases. also noticed a correlation with the streaming handshake delay in a subset of requests.
[01:12] Jordan: can you explain the streaming handshake bit again? is that Redwood's streaming or our infra?
[01:18] Priya: so streaming has two phases — initial first-chunk send (TTFT) and then chunk cadence. The handshake we call is the first network/frame exchange to start the stream; if the runtime has to warm a kernel path it can add 30–80ms. we suspect two causes: kernel selection latency + network microbursts in the region.
[01:36] Lina: we saw some network queueing events on our side at 02:59 where burst traffic from batch jobs congested egress. could be compounding.
[01:44] Alex: that suggests a mixed root cause — runtime selection + infra noise. Priya, you mentioned a hybrid kernel path for long sequences last week?
[01:50] Priya: yeah. the experiment is to pre-warm a quantized kernel for paths likely to go long — when seqlen estimate is > 1024 we route to kernel B which is slightly lower throughput but much lower start latency. for seqlen <1024 stick with the fast fused kernel A. On Friday we tried an auto-switch heuristic; it reduced p99 on long requests from 540ms to 260ms in the lab.
[02:10] Harold: lab numbers look promising — what's the cost trade-off? kernel B seems to be more mem-bound.
[02:16] Priya: approx +7% per-token from memory spill / less efficient matmuls, but net cost could be lower due to fewer hedging retries and lower SLA penalties. we're running a more realistic cost sim and I'll share the CSV.
[02:28] Jordan: and how does this interact with prefix/KV caching? if we can avoid cache misses, does kernel B still help?
[02:34] Priya: cache hits reduce the need for the long kernel, but some long prompts have fresh prefixes so cache can't help. Kernel B helps primarily during cold prefix or when attention patterns blow up memory.
[02:46] Lina: about the streaming jitter — are we talking packet loss or just scheduling jitter?
[02:50] Priya: looks like scheduling jitter plus occasional MTU fragmentation on a tiny subset of CDN edge nodes. we saw retransmits in the trace.
[02:58] Alex: so short term mitigation options: enable hedging (duplicate the first chunk across two paths), pre-warm the long-seqlen kernel on suspected requests, and adjust small-batch scheduling to avoid egress-burst alignment.
[03:10] Jordan: hedging sounds expensive; what's the cost impact?
[03:14] Priya: hedging the first chunk increases token compute ~ +12% for the hedged window but p99 improvements can be large; we'd only hedged top X% of traffic by seqlen or by traffic class.
[03:24] Harold: we can identify high-value requests to hedge — for example, verification flows with user wait times — and keep general queries unhedged.
[03:30] Alex: good approach. quick check on the shadow plan — NimbleScale will provide a ~2-hour production-like trace and Redwood will run a shadow with hybrid kernel + hedging enabled. agreed?
[03:39] Jordan: yes, we can do 10k requests, anonymized. we'll attach the trace to the shared drive.
[03:44] Alex: sweet. Priya, can you walk through the experiment matrix?
[03:47] Priya: sure — matrix has rows: kernel path (A/B/hybrid), hedging on/off, microbatch size (1/4/8), prefix cache TTL (0s/30s/300s). we'll run each combo for short windows and measure TTFT/p99 and cost. For seqlen buckets: <512, 512–1024, >1024.
[04:08] Lina: what's the expected timeline to get actionable numbers?
[04:12] Priya: we can run the prioritized matrix across the trace in less than 2 business days once we have the trace. I'll prioritize combos that look promising from Friday.
[04:20] Jordan: any risk of the shadow run affecting production?
[04:22] Alex: it's a non-invasive shadow — nothing writes to prod. network impact is minimal; we may want to co-ordinate maintenance windows.
[04:29] Harold: can Redwood share the instrumentation keys so we can map traces?
[04:32] Alex: yes — I'll share access to the benchmark sheet and the log correlation guide. link: https://redwood.internal/poc/nimblescale-harmonics (note: internal link placeholder)
[04:42] Priya: quick note on quantization: we saw a small accuracy drop when moving to 4-bit for kernel B on heavy seqlen examples; Harol, you'll want to validate generation quality on your eval set.
[04:55] Harold: will do, we'll run the eval prompt set overnight and report quality diffs tomorrow.
[04:59] Jordan: last night's spike — do we have any concrete prevention?
[05:03] Priya: immediate: set a conservative microbatch cap (2) during peak window, enable hedging for top 5% of seqlen traffic, and pre-warm kernel B during maintenance windows. Mid-term: smarter routing based on seqlen estimate and introducing backpressure signals from customer egress.
[05:20] Lina: can Redwood expose per-route token breakdown in console? would help us see who is causing long seqlen tails.
[05:26] Alex: yes, Redwood Console will show per-route token breakdown and we can add a custom dashboard for your seqlen buckets.
[05:30] Jordan: there's also procurement timeline — if POC looks good we plan to start Dedicated talks in Q3. not a firm commit but heads-up.
[05:38] Alex: noted. that helps prioritize SLA-oriented mitigations.
[05:41] Priya: ok next, quick demo of Friday's kernel warm trace — I'm going to share my screen but audio transcript has the highlights.
[05:47] [screen share noise / brief pause]
[06:05] Priya: in this trace you can see the runtime selects kernel A initially, then for requests estimated >1024 there's a warm transition — the wall clock shows a 40ms bump when kernel switches cold. the hybrid test keeps both warm and avoids the bump.
[06:24] Jordan: nice — what's the memory overhead to keep both warmed?
[06:28] Priya: about 15% extra GPU memory reserved per instance for the warmed kernels, so we'll need to size pools or do a best-effort warm on a subset of nodes.
[06:38] Harold: could we use a fast fallback to CPU for extremely rare long requests instead of keeping both warmed?
[06:42] Priya: possible but fallback to CPU kills latency — not ideal for TTFT. Might be acceptable for non-interactive batch flows.
[06:51] Lina: one more infra question: how does this play with our VPC peering? network path differences might change jitter profile.
[06:58] Alex: good point — we'll include a network traceroute log in the debug bundle. please attach your egress metrics slice for 02:30–03:30 so we can correlate.
[07:08] Jordan: will do.
[07:10] Priya: going to call out the prioritized experiment run list now: 1) hybrid kernel + hedging top 5% (short run on trace) 2) microbatching sweep (1/4/8) with prefix TTL variations 3) streaming handshake tuning (MTU, fragmentation checks) 4) quantization check on kernel B for quality.
[07:30] Harold: anything else on observability? we flagged a confusing trace last week where speaker labels were missing — makes debugging hard.
[07:36] Alex: yes we owe you a guide on trace correlation keys; I'll push that with the benchmark sheet.
[07:42] Jordan: curious — competitors like Anthropic offer slightly different streaming semantics, any risk we need to consider for our compliance or integration?
[07:50] Alex: not much; vendor semantics differ but the mitigation approaches (hedging, pre-warm) are the same. we'll focus on outcomes.
[07:57] Lina: ok planning — microburst shadow run window: prefer 6/9 or 6/10 mornings. Alex can you confirm your ops folks?
[08:05] Alex: I'll confirm with SE ops and flag 6/9 as first choice.
[08:09] Jordan: last thing — can Redwood provide a simple expected cost delta for enabling hedging on top 5% vs 10%? rough numbers ok.
[08:15] Priya: yes I'll include cost projections in the benchmark CSV — rough is fine for now.
[08:20] Alex: great. quick recap before we wrap: Redwood to share kernel-selection matrix + benchmark CSV (Priya), security pack and trace keys (Alex), NimbleScale to upload 10k trace and run eval on quantized generator (Jordan/Harold). schedule on-site microburst test week of 6/7; Alex to confirm by 6/2.
[08:42] Jordan: that sounds right. thanks all.
[08:45] Alex: thanks, we'll follow up in email with links. end.
